messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 49-year-old European-American City Council Member who served in combat and has been struggling with the aftermath of his traumatic experiences. Despite being married, John finds himself increasingly isolated from those around him due to the intense fears and intrusive memories that plague him daily. The trauma began during his time in combat when he witnessed and experienced events that left deep emotional scars. He often feels like parts of these memories are missing or unclear, making it hard for him to piece together a coherent picture of what happened. When John tries to recount these experiences, the narrative frequently falters, leaving him feeling frustrated and unable to explain the full scope of his trauma. This incomplete recollection exacerbates his distress because he is constantly left wondering about the details that are missing. This fragmented memory contributes significantly to his maladaptive strategies. Whenever he feels overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts or triggered by reminders of his combat experiences, John often turns up the volume on loud music or TV, seeking to drown out the overwhelming sensations and regain a sense of control. He has also become hypervigilant, constantly monitoring his own thoughts for signs that he is going crazy. This constant mental vigilance only adds to his stress, making it difficult for him to relax and trust his surroundings. John’s memories are so potent that they often lead to startle responses whenever someone touches him unexpectedly. Despite being in a safe environment, like his home or office, John cannot shake the feeling of danger. His wife has noticed how he flinches at even gentle touches, a reaction that strains their relationship and makes it hard for her to comfort him. The incomplete memories also fuel his negative appraisals about himself and the world around him. He believes that his body is an enemy, constantly reacting as if he were still in danger. This constant state of hypervigilance has led him to distrust the safety others assure him exists. Even when people tell John he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them because his body and mind are convinced otherwise. John’s maladaptive strategies have further entrenched these negative appraisals and memories. His reliance on sensory distraction to cope with intrusive thoughts only serves to amplify the fear and disconnection he feels. When he turns up the volume or distracts himself, the memories resurface even more vividly, making it difficult for him to trust that he is truly safe. The cycle of hypervigilance and memory distortion has significantly impacted his life as a City Council Member. John often finds himself avoiding social engagements and public appearances where physical contact might be expected or where he could be triggered by the crowded, unpredictable environments typical in city governance settings. His decision to avoid these situations stems from the fear that he cannot trust others’ assurances of safety. What finally brought John to seek help is the increasing isolation and strain on his marriage. He fears being trapped in this cycle indefinitely, unable to fully engage with life or reconnect with those around him. While he hopes for relief from his intrusive memories and a sense of safety, what frightens him most is the uncertainty about whether he can ever truly believe that he is safe. John’s journey towards recovery will involve addressing these interconnected symptoms, breaking the cycle of negative appraisals, and finding healthier ways to cope with his traumatic memories.
